title: Integrity under pressure: a simple way to decide

say: Integrity under pressure: a simple way to decide.
This is the video for module one of Ethics and Accountability at Work.
Ethics is the set of standards we use to decide what is right and fair when our choices affect other people: customers, colleagues, your employer, the members of your group.

panel.heading: Ethics and accountability, in plain words
items: Ethics: what is right and fair to others
Accountability: answering for what you did
Legal or common does not mean right
Integrity: the same person in every room

say: Accountability is the other half. It means being willing to answer for what you said you would do, what you actually did, and what happened, including your mistakes.

panel.heading: Ethics and accountability, in plain words
items: Ethics: what is right and fair to others
Accountability: answering for what you did
Legal or common does not mean right
Integrity: the same person in every room

say: Ethics is not the same as law or custom. Promising delivery on Friday when you know it will be Tuesday may be legal, but it is not honest. And things everybody does are not automatically right.

say: Integrity means your words and actions match, whether or not anyone is watching. A cashier with integrity counts the money the same way when the manager is away.

say: Accountability is something you can practise. First, own it: say, that was my responsibility.
Second, explain the facts, not excuses.
Third, repair what you can.
And fourth, prevent a repeat. A person who only owns, but never repairs, is sorry but not accountable.
For example, Amaka is a sales assistant in a Lagos pharmacy shop.

card.title: A small adjustment at month end
card.note: Report the true figure, with a note.

say: Her monthly target is 2,000,000 naira.

card.title: A small adjustment at month end
card.note: Report the true figure, with a note.

say: By the 30th she has reached about 1,850,000 naira. A colleague suggests recording next week's expected clinic order as this month's sale.
In plain words, that is recording a sale that has not happened. The owner would order the wrong stock and pay a bonus nobody earned.
So Amaka reports 1,850,000 naira, with a note that a confirmed clinic order is expected next week.

say: Most wrong choices are not made by bad people. They are made by ordinary people under pressure: a boss who wants a result, a relative asking a favour, a colleague saying we all do it. Watch for soft words like settle or adjust the figures.

say: Gifts are part of our culture. A token anyone could accept openly, like a calendar or a pack of biscuits, is usually fine.

panel.heading: When is a thank you too much?
right: Given while a decision is pending
You are asked to keep it quiet

say: For example, Ngozi buys supplies for a school in Enugu. A supplier whose contract is up for renewal sends a hamper with an envelope of 50,000 naira. She would not be comfortable if the proprietor saw it. That is her answer.
She returns the envelope with a polite note and tells the proprietor in writing. Cash from someone who wants something from you is almost always a bribe.

say: Some situations are dilemmas, where two things you care about pull apart. For example, Funmi is financial secretary of a 30-member cooperative in Ibadan.
Her friend Bisi has not paid for three months and asks to be marked as paid. Funmi pauses: friendship against fairness to 29 other members.

panel.heading: Five steps to decide
items: Pause: name the values in conflict

say: She gets the facts. Bisi owes 15,000 naira, and a false entry could let her take a loan she is not entitled to.

panel.heading: Five steps to decide
items: Pause: name the values in conflict

say: She lists three options, not two: mark her paid, refuse and say nothing, or refuse and help Bisi ask for a written payment plan.

panel.heading: Five steps to decide
items: Pause: name the values in conflict

say: She chooses the third, and tells Bisi kindly: I can't write what didn't happen, but I'll come with you to ask for a plan.

panel.heading: Five steps to decide
items: Pause: name the values in conflict

say: She follows up. The executive approves a plan, Funmi records each payment exactly, and Bisi clears the balance in six months.

panel.rule: Separate what you know from what you assume.

say: Doing right can carry real costs, so protect yourself. Keep dated notes and save messages. Raise concerns in writing with the right person, and find a trusted ally.
Never confront a powerful person alone. If anyone threatens you, leave, keep the evidence, and seek help from people who can protect you.

panel.heading: When doing right is risky
items: Raise concerns in writing, through proper channels
Never confront a powerful person alone
If threatened, leave and seek help

say: Your practice. Write down three soft words used around you, and what they really describe. Write two polite refusal scripts and practise them aloud. Then work one real dilemma through the five steps, with a facts column and an assumptions column.
Now continue with the lessons below.
